title: State (BSES YPL) v. Mohd. Riyaz (FIR 65/2020)
court: Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
result: Convicted under Section 135, Electricity Act, 2003; civil liability settled during trial but amount not deposited; posted for hearing on sentence
statutes: Third proviso to Section 135(1) Electricity Act 2003

interpretations.interpretation: Hooking a cable directly onto the licensee's pole to feed premises with no meter of their own is the paradigm clause (a) offence; 'dishonestly' takes its s.24 IPC meaning — unmetered floors, the pole-to-premises cable and no lawful-source explanation satisfied it.

A reverse-onus clause: proof of an artificial or unauthorised means of abstraction raises a presumption of dishonest use 'until the contrary is proved'. 'Shall presume' is a compulsory presumption (Neeraj Dutt); the accused must adduce evidence making his defence reasonably probable to a prudent man (Hiten P. Dalal); the natural rebuttal is proof of a lawful, metered source, typically paid bills, the onus lying on the consumer under Section 106 Evidence Act (Mukesh Rastogi).

citations.case: Balu Sudam Khalde v. State of Maharashtra
citations.principle: Incriminating suggestions put by defence counsel in cross-examination bind the accused and can establish facts such as the factum of, and presence at, the inspection.

citations.case: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashwani Kumar
citations.principle: An inspection report prepared by officers in discharge of official duty carries a presumption of regularity; onus on the consumer to rebut by cogent evidence.

citations.case: Sushil Sharma v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Non-examination of an independent/public witness is no infirmity where inspecting officials are trustworthy and bear no enmity to the accused.
'Shall presume' denotes a compulsory legal presumption the court is bound to draw until the fact is disproved.

citations.case: Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee
citations.principle: Rebuttal of a statutory presumption need not be conclusive; evidence must make the defence reasonably probable to a prudent man.

citations.case: Mukesh Rastogi v. North Delhi Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Easiest rebuttal of the theft presumption is production of paid electricity bills; Section 106 Evidence Act places that onus on the consumer.

significance.point: Unmetered occupation plus a pole tap is the paradigm s.135(1)(a) case
significance.explanation: Where whole floors run with no meter and a cable traces to the licensee's pole, the offence is made out on the inspection evidence itself.

significance.point: Mass-raid testimony elicited by the defence proved the inspection
significance.explanation: Answers the defence itself drew out — that the premises were inspected in a mass raid and the load report prepared on observation — bound the accused (Balu Sudam Khalde).

significance.point: A 65B certificate, where filed, forecloses the videography challenge
significance.explanation: With the certificate on record (Ex.PW4/A), the bare suggestion of fabrication had nothing to bite on — contrast companion cases resting on the waived-objection rule (Sonu @ Amar).

significance.point: A bill in someone else's name is no rebuttal
significance.explanation: The only electricity bill on record stood in the wife's name; under the s.106 onus (Mukesh Rastogi) the accused had to show paid bills for lawful supply to these premises.

significance.point: Settlement corroborates guilt even if never paid
significance.explanation: Settling the theft bill while pleading inability to deposit was read as conduct inconsistent with innocence.

generic_facts.theft_mode: direct theft / pole hooking — two-core cable from BSES pole feeding unmetered 1st & 2nd floors
generic_facts.premises: two residential floors of a house, resettlement colony
generic_facts.meter_status: no meter for inspected floors; ground-floor meter served ground floor only
generic_facts.ownership_evidence: electricity bill on record in wife's name; premises identity in video undisputed
key_evidence: seized two-core cable (2x10 sq mm, ~0.5 m) identified in court
generic_facts.defence: bare denial and false implication via amicus curiae; no defence evidence; settled civil liability but did not deposit (financial constraints)
